children: By Emese Bartha

The recent hefty selling in U.S. Treasurys that sent their yields soaring to multiyear highs may have gone too far, and this could provide opportunities for longer-term investors seeking good levels of return, said Charles Tan, chief investment officer of global fixed income at American Century Investments.
Long-dated Treasurys have suffered intense selling in recent weeks. On Monday, 10- and 30-year yields hit levels not seen in 24 years at 5.349% and 5.703%, respectively, according to Tradeweb data.

Tan considers a 5.25% yield on the 10-year Treasury an appealing entry point, particularly for long-term institutional buyers managing long-duration liabilities, including insurance companies, pension plans, and endowment funds. The 10-year Treasury yield last traded at 5.281%.

The last leg of the recent Treasury selling reflected a number of technical factors, including forced selling by some investors ahead of the end of the third quarter as yields surpassed key levels, he said.
Some hedge funds and fast-money investors were caught out and forced to rapidly adjust their positions in Treasurys, Tan said.

"The forced unwinding triggered some cascading trades through mortgage convexity hedging, insurance companies and real money asset managers reducing duration exposure at quarter-end when liquidity was more constrained." Overall selling pressure "was intense but not chaotic," he said.

Tan considers that the main factor behind the recent surge in Treasury yields was the massive increase in competition for long-term capital. Requirements for substantial borrowing to fund huge artificial-intelligence investment and infrastructure projects have come alongside ever-increasing borrowing needs from governments across major developed economies.

"This is happening at a time when the global savings glut is unwinding as the global trade frictions, tariffs and U.S.-Iran war are reshaping the global trade order and the associated capital flows," he said.

He expects, however, that the boom in AI-related debt could slow in future as credit markets become significantly more disciplined regarding mega-cap technology financing. This would likely result in fewer interest-rate hikes from the Federal Reserve than markets currently expect.
"The projected multi-trillion AI spending is unrealistic as more and more investors question the underlying economics. There will be a buyers' strike."

Cracks are already beginning to surface in lower-tier credit, notably within CCC-rated high-yield corporate bonds, as well as in interest-rate-sensitive stock sectors including financials, utilities, and consumer names, he said.
A slowdown in the AI credit boom "reduces the need for the Fed to hike," Tan said, adding that current market pricing for up to four rate increases over the next year was overly aggressive.
Inflation and debt fears have been secondary factors behind higher Treasury yields.

"Inflation was clearly not the main driver, despite the headlines," Tan said. "Nor was concern over the U.S. government's creditworthiness or much talked about dollar debasement, because the U.S. term premium is only about 100 basis points, right in the middle of its 40-year range, and lower than many other developed-market countries."
The term premium is the additional return investors demand for buying longer-dated over shorter-dated debt.

Market expectations have already shifted away from anticipating additional monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve later this month. U.S. money markets show that markets now assign a probability of just 19% to a 25-basis-point rate hike at the Fed's next decision on Oct. 28, down sharply from 70% at the start of last week.
Tan agrees with this outlook.

"I think it makes sense for the Fed to pause in October and assess the upcoming data," he said. "The fact is the sharp rise in rates in recent months is already tightening financial conditions and has done some heavy lifting for the Fed."
American Century Investments' assets under management totaled $350 billion as of Sept. 30, 2026.
